#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# The estimator, the menu, its validation and the helpers of Tasks 4 to 6, as
# in R/spec_tools.R of the IDE workspace, apart from the tag of the class chart,
# which lasts for the browser session. The data files arrive through the
# resources list of the including page, in the folder named by .data_dir.

# ============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION – the class chart and the workshop's website
# ============================================================================
# The results Form pre-filled by submit_exploration() and report_result(): its
# ID and the entry codes of its seven fields, shared by the workshop; a Form of
# its own replaces them here only. .case_word follows the tag in every label,
# and the chart of this case study reads only the rows that carry it.
.form_id <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
.form_entry <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
                 t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
                 r = "entry.1660273001")
.case_word <- "housing"
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing"
# ============================================================================


# ---- The estimator -------------------------------------------------------------
# A verbatim copy of R/_tools.R in the workshop's GitHub repository, which builds
# the curve; the IDE workspace carries the same copy in R/spec_tools.R.

# The IDE workspace, the webR workspace and the workshop's pipeline run the
# same code. R/check_parity.R in the workshop's GitHub repository checks the HC2 errors
# and the average marginal effect against estimatr and margins.

# The options of the curve, in menu order. Anything else is refused by
# check_spec() with the reason recorded in data/menu_options.csv.
SPEC_AXES <- list(
  comparison = c("white", "nonhispanic"),
  population = c("replies", "all"),
  uncoded    = c("drop", "not_named"),
  model      = c("lpm", "logit"),
  adjust     = c("none", "email", "place", "place_ethnic")
)

# Covariates of each adjustment set; all are recorded before the emails went out.
ADJUST_TERMS <- list(
  none         = character(0),
  email        = "hard_email",
  place        = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third"),
  place_ethnic = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")
)

# The analysed rows and the outcome of one specification. Bounced emails never
# reached an official and are outside the experiment under every option.
spec_frame <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") {
  housing |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply),
                  .env$comparison == "nonhispanic" | group %in% c("white", "hispanic"),
                  .env$population == "all" | reply == 1) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
      y = dplyr::case_when(reply == 0 ~ 0,
                           is.na(named) & .env$uncoded == "not_named" ~ 0,
                           .default = named)
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(y))
}

# The conversion rules of the robustness study (standard_correlation_coefficient.R in
# github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100): t with its df, which is the rule of
# effectsize::t_to_r(); z with the sample size standing in for the missing df;
# a chi-square read as the square of a z, so it carries no sign.
r_robustness <- function(stat, stat_type, df, n) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    stat_type == "t" ~ effectsize::t_to_r(stat, df, ci = NULL)$r,
    stat_type == "z" ~ tanh(abs(stat) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3))) * sign(stat),
    stat_type == "chi2" ~ tanh(sqrt(abs(stat)) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3)))
  )
}

check_spec <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  chosen <- list(comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
                 model = model, adjust = adjust)
  bad <- names(chosen)[!purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, SPEC_AXES[names(chosen)], \(v, ok) v %in% ok)]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("Not on the curve: ", paste0(bad, " = '", unlist(chosen[bad]), "'", collapse = ", "),
         ". The options are listed in data/menu_options.csv.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# One specification: estimate in percentage points (negative = Hispanic names
# greeted by name less often, the direction of the claim), its SE and 95%
# interval, the test of the model that the specification fits, and the partial
# correlation by the rule of the robustness study.
fit_spec <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none") {
  check_spec(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
  # the data of the replication hold no hard_email, which the adjustment
  # leaves out
  terms <- intersect(ADJUST_TERMS[[adjust]], names(housing))
  # only the model columns, and only the emails with every covariate;
  # marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
  frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison, population, uncoded) |>
    dplyr::select("y", "hisp", dplyr::all_of(terms)) |>
    stats::na.omit()
  form <- stats::reformulate(c("hisp", terms), response = "y")

  if (model == "lpm") {
    fit <- stats::lm(form, data = frame)
    # HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from sandwich::vcovHC() (Zeileis
    # 2004, Journal of Statistical Software), with the t test on the residual df
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "t", stat = row$t,
                 df = row$df_error, p = row$p)
    est <- list(b = row$Coefficient, se = row$SE, low = row$CI_low, high = row$CI_high)
  } else {
    fit <- stats::glm(form, family = stats::binomial(), data = frame)
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, ci_method = "wald")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "z", stat = row$z,
                 df = NA_real_, p = row$p)
    # The average marginal effect: the mean over the analysed emails of the
    # predicted probability with a Hispanic name minus that with a comparison
    # name, with delta-method errors (marginaleffects; Arel-Bundock, Greifer and
    # Heiss 2024, Journal of Statistical Software)
    ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
    est <- list(b = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error, low = ame$conf.low, high = ame$conf.high)
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
    model = model, adjust = adjust,
    b_pp = 100 * est$b, se_pp = 100 * est$se,
    coef = test$coef, coef_se = test$coef_se,
    stat_type = test$stat_type, stat = test$stat, df = test$df, p = test$p,
    r = r_robustness(test$stat, test$stat_type, test$df, nrow(frame)),
    n = nrow(frame), n_hisp = sum(frame$hisp == 1), n_comp = sum(frame$hisp == 0),
    rate_hisp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 1]),
    rate_comp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 0]),
    ci_low = 100 * est$low, ci_high = 100 * est$high
  )
}

# The free-text label that carries a specification to the class chart.
spec_line <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  sprintf("comparison=%s population=%s uncoded=%s model=%s adjust=%s",
          comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
}


# ---- The menu --------------------------------------------------------------------
# The eleven decisions in menu order, with the options on the curve: those of
# the five decisions of SPEC_AXES multiply to the 64 specifications, and the
# other six keep one each. Every other option is a row of data/menu_options.csv,
# with its reason.
.menu <- list(
  # The question
  outcome    = "named",
  comparison = SPEC_AXES$comparison,
  population = SPEC_AXES$population,
  names      = "both",
  officials  = "any",
  # Measurement
  uncoded    = SPEC_AXES$uncoded,
  bounced    = "exclude",
  # The model
  model      = SPEC_AXES$model,
  adjust     = SPEC_AXES$adjust,
  inference  = "model",
  scale      = "pp"
)
.level_titles <- c(estimand    = "The question",
                   measurement = "Measurement",
                   estimation  = "The model")


# ---- The shipped files -----------------------------------------------------------
# Each file is read once and cached. An empty cell must read as NA: the 14
# authorities without community thirds would otherwise enter the adjusted
# models as a fourth level "".
.cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.read_once <- function(name, path) {
  if (is.null(.cache[[name]])) {
    if (!file.exists(path))
      stop(sprintf("%s not found. Reload the page.",
                   path), call. = FALSE)
    assign(name, utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8",
                                 na.strings = c("", "NA")),
           envir = .cache)
  }
  .cache[[name]]
}
.housing   <- function() .read_once("housing", file.path(.data_dir, "housing_emails.csv"))
.curve   <- function() .read_once("curve", file.path(.data_dir, "spec_curve.csv"))
.options <- function() .read_once("options", file.path(.data_dir, "menu_options.csv"))


# ---- Pages on the workshop's website ----------------------------------------------------
.pages <- c(
  "background.qmd"                = "Background",
  "menu.qmd"                      = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#map"                  = "Decision map",
  "curve.qmd"                     = "Specification curve",
  "companion/experiments.qmd"     = "Audit experiments",
  "companion/binary-outcomes.qmd" = "Binary outcomes",
  "companion/dags.qmd"            = "Causal graphs and conditioning",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"      = "The multiverse and its critics")
.page_ref <- function(path) {
  title <- if (path %in% names(.pages)) .pages[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub(".qmd", ".html", path, fixed = TRUE))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}


# ---- Validation ------------------------------------------------------------------
# .validate() checks a named list, the arguments of try_spec(); .check_choices()
# reads the eleven my_* choices of the preregistration block. An option off the
# curve stops with its reason from menu_options.csv, the page that teaches it
# and the options on the curve.
.on_menu <- function(axis, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[axis]]

.refuse <- function(axis, v, as_args) {
  shown <- if (as_args) axis else paste0("my_", axis)
  keep  <- .menu[[axis]]
  map   <- paste0("  All decisions and options: ", .page_ref("menu.qmd#map"))
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".", shown, shown, keep[1]),
         call. = FALSE)
  opts <- .options()
  row  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, .data$option == .env$v)
  off  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, !.data$on_curve)$option
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("Not on the curve of %d specifications: %s = \"%s\" (%s).",
            nrow(.curve()), shown, v, row$label),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    paste0("  Taught in: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s = %s.", shown, .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown, v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(keep, collapse = " | ")),
    if (length(off) > 0)
      sprintf("  Off the curve, refused with a reason: %s.", paste(off, collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(a) .on_menu(a, ch[[a]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], as_args)
  ch[names(.menu)]
}

# The choices are looked up from the frame of this function outwards, which
# reaches the session in which the preregistration block was run.
.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- paste0("my_", names(.menu))
  ch <- mget(need, envir = environment(), inherits = TRUE, ifnotfound = list(NULL))
  missing <- need[purrr::map_lgl(ch, is.null)]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice of the preregistration block and run the block.", call. = FALSE)
  .validate(stats::setNames(ch, names(.menu)))
}


# ---- The live fit ----------------------------------------------------------------
# fit_spec() on the five decisions that vary on the curve, with its 95%
# interval (t for the linear model, normal for the average marginal effect of
# the logit) and its place among the 64, checked against its row of
# data/spec_curve.csv.
.result <- function(ch) {
  fit <- fit_spec(.housing(), ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .curve()
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model,
                          .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1) {
    warning("This specification has no row in data/spec_curve.csv; reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  } else if (abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6 || abs(fit$stat - stored$stat) > 1e-6) {
    warning(sprintf("The fit (%.4f points, %s = %.4f) differs from data/spec_curve.csv (%.4f points, %s = %.4f). Reload the page.",
                    fit$b_pp, fit$stat_type, fit$stat, stored$b_pp, fit$stat_type, stored$stat),
            call. = FALSE)
  }
  c(fit, list(further = sum(curve$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(curve)))
}


# ---- The printout ----------------------------------------------------------------
.comparison_label <- function(comparison)
  c(white = "white names", nonhispanic = "white and Black names")[[comparison]]

.fmt_p <- function(p) sprintf("= %s", format(signif(p, 2), scientific = FALSE))

.class_line <- function(res) {
  below <- res$b_pp < 0
  sig   <- res$p < 0.05
  if (below && sig) "below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim"
  else if (below) "below zero, but not significant at 5%"
  else if (sig) "above zero and significant at 5%, against the direction of the claim"
  else "above zero and not significant at 5%"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL) {
  unit <- if (ch$population == "all") "delivered emails" else "replies"
  test <- if (res$stat_type == "t") c(
    sprintf("  Test: t = %.2f on %d df, p %s (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)",
            res$stat, round(res$df), .fmt_p(res$p))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("  Test: z = %.2f, p %s (logistic regression; the difference is its average marginal effect)",
            res$stat, .fmt_p(res$p)),
    sprintf("        logit coefficient %.3f, standard error %.3f", res$coef, res$coef_se)
  )
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", spec_line(ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust)),
    sprintf("  Greeted by name: Hispanic names %.1f%% of %d %s, %s %.1f%% of %d",
            res$rate_hisp, res$n_hisp, unit, .comparison_label(ch$comparison), res$rate_comp,
            res$n_comp),
    sprintf("  Difference: %.2f percentage points, 95%% interval %.2f to %.2f",
            res$b_pp, res$ci_low, res$ci_high),
    test,
    sprintf("  n = %d %s, partial r = %.3f (the conversion rule of the robustness study)", res$n, unit, res$r),
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %d of the %d specifications have an estimate further below zero",
            res$further, res$n_curve)))
  invisible(res)
}


# ---- Task 4: the exploratory helpers -----------------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

# The first five arguments vary on the curve; the other six are fixed on it,
# and any other option of theirs is refused with its reason.
try_spec <- function(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none", outcome = "named", names = "both",
                     officials = "any", bounced = "exclude", inference = "model", scale = "pp") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, comparison = comparison, population = population,
                       names = names, officials = officials, uncoded = uncoded,
                       bounced = bounced, model = model, adjust = adjust,
                       inference = inference, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b_pp = res$b_pp, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,
                    stat_type = res$stat_type, stat = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", dplyr::bind_rows(.tried$log, row), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The log of every fit of try_spec(), with only the decisions that varied.
my_experiments <- function() {
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet. Run try_spec() first.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  varied <- purrr::keep(names(.menu), \(a) dplyr::n_distinct(d[[a]]) > 1)
  show <- d |>
    dplyr::transmute(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(varied)),
                     estimate = round(.data$b_pp, 2),
                     interval = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", .data$ci_low, .data$ci_high),
                     test = sprintf("%s = %.2f", .data$stat_type, .data$stat),
                     p = signif(.data$p, 2),
                     n = .data$n)
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications tried: %d (estimates in percentage points)\n", nrow(d)))
  # wide enough for all five varied decisions on one line
  old_width <- options(width = max(getOption("width"), 120))
  on.exit(options(old_width))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nEstimates from %.2f to %.2f points  |  below zero and significant at 5%%: %d of %d",
                     min(d$b_pp), max(d$b_pp), sum(d$b_pp < 0 & d$p < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

# prereg() prints the block and returns it, so that run_spec() can check that
# the block has not changed since.
prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  rows <- .options() |>
    dplyr::filter(paste(.data$axis, .data$option) %in% paste(names(ch), unlist(ch))) |>
    dplyr::arrange(match(.data$axis, names(.menu))) |>
    dplyr::mutate(line = sprintf("    %-31s : %-12s (%s)", .data$decision, .data$option, .data$label))
  block <- purrr::imap(.level_titles, \(title, lv) c(paste0("  ", title), rows$line[rows$level == lv])) |>
    unlist(use.names = FALSE)
  ph <- stats::setNames(rows$phrase, rows$axis)
  statement <- c(
    sprintf("%s%s, %s, %s, the difference in the share that drew %s between Hispanic names and %s (%s, %s).",
            toupper(substr(ph[["population"]], 1, 1)), substring(ph[["population"]], 2),
            ph[["names"]], ph[["officials"]], ph[["outcome"]], ph[["comparison"]],
            ph[["uncoded"]], ph[["bounced"]]),
    sprintf("Estimated with %s, %s, tested by %s and reported %s.",
            ph[["model"]], ph[["adjust"]], ph[["inference"]], ph[["scale"]]))
  writeLines(c(
    "DECLARED – the preregistered specification:",
    "",
    block,
    "",
    "  The estimand statement",
    strwrap(statement, width = 78, indent = 4, exdent = 4),
    "",
    "run_spec() and report_result() read these choices."))
  invisible(structure(list(choices = ch), class = "housing_prereg"))
}

run_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "housing_prereg"))
    stop("Pass the object that prereg() returned: my_spec <- prereg(), then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!identical(spec$choices, .check_choices()))
    stop("The choices have changed since prereg(). Run the block and my_spec <- prereg() again, then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  .print_result(spec$choices, .result(spec$choices), "Preregistered specification:")
}

report_result <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  .submit(ch, .result(ch), "declared",

}


# ---- Task 6: the replication --------------------------------------------------------
# replicate_spec() fits the declared specification on the data of the
# replication, translated to the new experiment (no Black names, no reply
# without a greeting code, no hard_email) with each change printed, checks the
# fit against data/replication_curve.csv and places it among the 12
# specifications to which the 64 collapse on the new data.
replicate_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "housing_prereg"))
    stop("Pass the object that prereg() returned: my_spec <- prereg(), then replicate_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  ch <- spec$choices
  new <- utils::modifyList(ch, list(comparison = "white", uncoded = "drop",
                                    adjust = if (ch$adjust == "email") "none" else ch$adjust))
  changes <- c(
    if (ch$comparison == "nonhispanic")
      "  comparison = \"white\": the new experiment used no Black names.",
    if (ch$uncoded == "not_named")
      "  uncoded = \"drop\": every reply of the new experiment carries a greeting code.",
    if (ch$adjust != "none")
      "  adjust: without hard_email, which the new data do not hold.")
  fit <- fit_spec(.read_once("replication", file.path(.data_dir, "housing_replication.csv")),
                  new$comparison, new$population, new$uncoded, new$model, new$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .read_once("replication_curve", file.path(.data_dir, "replication_curve.csv"))
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model, .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1 || abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6)
    warning("The fit on the new data differs from data/replication_curve.csv. Reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  distinct <- dplyr::filter(curve, !duplicated(.data$rep_spec))
  .print_result(ch, .result(ch), "Declared specification on the original data:")
  writeLines(c("", "Declared specification on the data of the replication:",
               if (length(changes) > 0) changes
               else "  No translation: every choice exists in the new data."))
  .print_result(new, c(fit, list(further = sum(distinct$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(distinct))))
}

# A fresh tag, drawn without touching the random-number stream of the session.
.new_tag <- function() {
  had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  if (had_seed) old_seed <- get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
  on.exit(if (had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = globalenv())

# A nickname reduced to lower-case ASCII letters, digits and single hyphens,
# at most 24 characters – the only form that the class chart parses.
.clean_tag <- function(x) {
  # iconv on Windows turns these into "?": the Romanian comma-below letters and the eszett
  x <- gsub("ß", "ss", chartr("ȘșȚț", "SsTt", trimws(as.character(x)[1])))
  ascii <- suppressWarnings(iconv(x, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"))
  if (!is.na(ascii)) x <- ascii
  x <- gsub("^-+|-+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x)))
  x <- gsub("-+$", "", substr(x, 1, 24))
  if (is.na(x) || !nzchar(x))
    stop("A nickname needs at least one letter or digit, for example nickname = \"blue-heron\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  x
}

# The tag of this session: the nickname if one is given, otherwise the tag
# already drawn, otherwise a fresh one. Returns the tag and the one it replaced.
.class_tag <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  stored <- .tag_env$tag
  tag <- if (!is.null(nickname)) .clean_tag(nickname) else if (!is.null(stored)) stored else .new_tag()
  assign("tag", tag, envir = .tag_env)
  list(tag = tag, replaced = if (!is.null(stored) && !identical(tag, stored)) stored)
}

make_dag <- function(..., exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official") {

## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
I want to start with a question that is seldom asked out loud, namely what we are doing when we do social science. We make claims about the world that could turn out to be wrong, together with some statement of how we would find out. And we publish a claim so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it and build on it. Science depends on that handover, since a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. When we ask whether social science is in trouble, then, the question is quite specific: whether the handover works, and whether someone else can pick a finding up and do something with it.
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take them in the order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: with small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false without anybody breaking a rule. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn then demonstrated it in 2011, showing that the flexibility that researchers legitimately have can push a false-positive rate of five per cent above sixty. They made the point by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes people younger. Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake off, which is that you do not need to run many tests for this to happen, because a single test chosen after looking at the data already has the wrong p-value.
:::

::: {.small}

Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes

Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result, against thirty-six per cent of the replications, and the effect sizes came back at about half their original size; this is the study that took the phrase 'replication crisis' out of methodology seminars. ## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start, your code, your data or your materials, and open research is a set of practices that supply such things, each removing a specific obstacle. Open data let someone else reanalyse your evidence, open code lets them rerun your exact analysis, and open materials let them run the study again in a new sample. Open access lets them read the paper at all, which sounds trivial until you try to obtain a paper from outside a wealthy university. A preregistration is a dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist, and a registered report goes further, since the plan is peer-reviewed and the decision to publish is taken before any result exists. [advance] None of these practices guards against every problem, and Munafò and colleagues set out the whole programme at length.
:::

## The two tasks of the robustness study {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages. Task one left the analysis entirely to the analyst, who then recorded one of four conclusions: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived, asking for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, with a short instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict, and task two whether they produce the same number, a question that can only be asked once everyone answers roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms, since each analyst reports the statistic that their model produces, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. The robustness study converted these statistics onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on one axis. A panel of peers also judged whether each analysis was appropriate for the claim, so the spread that the study reports is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted: that they estimate the same quantity, and that each conversion counts the units that carry the evidence. Much of what follows today concerns what happens when the first of these does not hold.
:::

X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.

::: notes
The causal graph is the second of those three steps, and these three small graphs hold all the graph theory that the tasks need. In every panel the green arrow is the effect of X on Y that you are after. A confounder is a common cause of the predictor and the outcome, and its red fork is a back-door path that biases the estimate while it stays open, so you adjust for the confounder to close it. A mediator lies on the causal path, and its amber path is part of the total effect, so adjusting for it removes part of what you want to measure. ## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}


::: {.cell}

::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust for the variable in its middle. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened when you adjust for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.

::: notes
A causal graph is read through its paths, since association flows along every open path between X and Y and not only along the causal arrow. The work consists in finding which paths are open and closing the ones that you do not want, and two rules do all of it. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting for the variable in the middle, as with the red back-door fork on the left. A path through a collider is closed by default, and adjusting for the collider opens it. The back-door criterion puts the two rules together: close every path that enters X from behind, and leave the causal path from X to Y alone. Only an adjustment set that does both gives an estimate that can be read as causal.
:::

The second is reverse causation and feedback. In a panel, which follows the same people or places over time, today's outcome can feed tomorrow's predictor, and adjusting for the stable differences between units does not on its own deal with a confounder that changes over time or with a feedback loop. A randomised experiment avoids this second problem by design, because nothing that happens later can change who received which treatment.

Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is **post-treatment conditioning**: the gap among replies mixes an effect on **how** officials write with a difference in **which** officials wrote [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment; @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias].

::: notes
Now draw a box around the reply, because that is what the paper does when it compares greetings among the replies only. The reply is caused by the name and also by the official, so it is a common effect of the two, a collider, and conditioning on a collider opens a path between its causes. If a Hispanic name discourages some officials from replying, the officials who answered Santiago are a different mix from those who answered Brett, perhaps the more conscientious ones, perhaps the less busy ones, and their habits of greeting then travel along the red path into the comparison. [advance] The general name for this is post-treatment conditioning, conditioning on something that the treatment can change, and it can produce a gap even where the name has no effect on tone at all. Coppock wrote about it for exactly this kind of audit experiment.
:::

## Counting every delivered email {#counting-every-delivered-email .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Count **every delivered email**, with no reply counted as no greeting: no box, nothing opened, and the groups stay as randomisation made them
- The outcome changes with it: a **reply that greets the sender by name**, which combines whether a reply came with how it began
:::

::: {.small}
| Emails counted | Hispanic names | White names | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coded replies (n = 362) | 41.2% | 61.1% | −19.97 points |
| Delivered emails (n = 662) | 21.6% | 35.0% | −13.34 points |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two defensible questions. Among the replies: the question of the claim, about tone, but an effect of the name alone only if the name did not change who replied. Among all emails: an effect of the name that randomisation protects, on a different outcome. The reply gap of −4.8 points (p = 0.214) makes a large selection unlikely, without ruling it out.
:::

::: notes
The remedy is to remove the box: count every email that arrived, and treat an email without a reply as one without a greeting. Nothing is then conditioned on, and the groups are as the random number generator made them. The outcome, however, changes with the denominator, and becomes a reply that greets the sender by name, which combines whether a reply came with how it began. Among the replies the shares are forty-one against sixty-one per cent, a gap of twenty points, and among all delivered emails twenty-two against thirty-five, a gap of thirteen. [advance] Neither comparison is wrong. The comparison among replies answers the question of the claim, about tone, and gives the effect of the name alone only if the name did not change who replied. The comparison among all emails is protected by the design, and answers a related but different question. One of the five analysts, 25N5D, made exactly this choice.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
8PTRZ, the replies with a code:

:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
For a two-by-two table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the **continuity correction** unless told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring. 8PTRZ and 25N5D kept the default, and so did you. For 25N5D the test gives 13.683 with it and 14.334 without it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A reproduction depends on the **defaults and the codings of the software** as well as on the data and the model. The *z* of EWFMI is positive because its model takes the Hispanic names as the base group.
:::

::: notes
The first line of the printout of chisq dot test, which most people skip, reads Pearson's chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction. [advance] For a two-by-two table R applies that correction by default, in chisq dot test and in prop dot test alike: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring, which makes the test a little more cautious. Without it, 8PTRZ gets fourteen point nine five and 25N5D fourteen point three three. Both analysts kept the default, and so did you, which is why your values match the record to the third decimal. [advance] The coding matters in the same way, since EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, and its z is positive for that reason. A script that relies on a default is reproducible only for as long as the default stays the same.

## Standard errors for a 0/1 outcome {#standard-errors-for-a-binary-outcome .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- The variance of a 0/1 outcome is *p*(1 − *p*), so it differs between groups whose shares differ
- **Conventional** standard errors assume one common variance; **HC2** errors, one of the 'heteroskedasticity-consistent' or 'robust' errors, let each group keep its own
- For a comparison of two groups, the HC2 error is, to within a hair, the standard error of a difference between two independent proportions
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On the reference comparison the two agree: HC2 **5.16** points, conventional **5.17**. With covariates or very unequal groups they part, which is why the curve uses HC2 throughout.
:::

::: notes
The standard errors appear on the menu as well. When the outcome is nought or one, its variance is the share times one minus the share, so groups with different shares have different variances. Conventional regression errors assume one common variance, which a linear probability model breaks by construction, while HC2 errors, one member of the family usually called robust errors, let each group keep its own variance, and for a simple comparison of two groups they come out almost exactly as the textbook standard error of a difference between two proportions. [advance] On our reference comparison the two kinds agree to within a hundredth of a point, because the groups are similar in size and in share. With covariates, or with groups of very different sizes, the two kinds of error can part, so the curve uses HC2 throughout.
:::

## Covariates in an experiment {#covariates-in-an-experiment .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- Randomisation balances the communities across the names in expectation, so covariates are **not needed to remove bias**
- They can make an estimate more **precise**, if they predict the outcome
- On the curve, against no covariates: the hard-to-find address moves the estimate by 0.08 points on average, the size and poverty of the community by 0.95, and with its ethnic composition by 1.06 – partly because 14 emails lack the community thirds
- The continuous census values of the paper are **not in the public file**, because they would identify the authorities
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The instruction of the robustness study to leave out ethnic composition therefore changes very little on these data.
:::

::: notes
In an observational study covariates are how we try to remove confounding, but in an experiment their job is different. Randomisation already balances the communities across the six names in expectation, so covariates are not needed to remove bias, and at most they make an estimate more precise, if they predict the outcome. On the curve, adding the hard-to-find address moves the estimate by less than a tenth of a point, and adding the size, poverty and ethnic composition of the community moves it by about one point, partly because fourteen emails lack the community data and drop out. The continuous census values of the paper are not available at all, since the public file gives only thirds. [advance] The one instruction of the robustness study, to leave out ethnic composition, therefore changes very little here.
:::

## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Multiverse background, 2 slides – skip to the curve →](#the-curve-of-the-claim)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – developed for *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Under all these names the proposal is the same: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
The vocabulary is a mess, and knowing where each word came from helps. Multiverse analysis comes from Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of choices in processing the data, how a variable is coded, which cases are excluded and how items are combined, with the proposal that the whole set of datasets that those choices could have produced be reported. Specification curve analysis, from Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, makes the same move for the choices of model and adds a way of drawing it, with the estimates on top and, beneath them, the choices that produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea, reached independently in epidemiology, and there is now a book-length treatment by Young and Cumberworth with computational recipes. [advance] Under their different names, they all propose that analytical choices be enumerated rather than left invisible.
:::

## Critics of the multiverse {#the-multiverse-has-its-critics .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. This workshop's curve keeps only the specifications that a review of every option judged justifiable for the claim, and setting each option beside its twins does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your preregistered specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that preregistering a choice does not yet make it *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. The full menu serves **reflection** and the curve of the claim moves towards **persuasion**; how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis of the red-card study: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The method that you have practised is the subject of a live debate. Katrin Auspurg, who with Josef Brüderl traced the spread in the red-card study to teams that answered different questions, replied to a study of about three point six billion estimates that only thoughtful and justified models belong in a curve, and the curve of this workshop keeps only the options of the menu that were judged justifiable answers to the claim. Lakens and colleagues argue that once the question is fixed only one analysis implements it correctly, and their point that preregistering a choice does not make it justified is why the causal graph comes before the preregistration. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask whether a multiverse is meant for reflection, persuasion or inference, each of which needs a differently built set; the full menu serves reflection, and the curve, with a published reason for every option, moves towards persuasion. [advance]
:::

## The one-correct-analysis argument {#there-is-only-one-correct-analysis .smaller}

::: {.small}
The argument from Lakens and colleagues runs in four steps:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument most of the spread is error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
The strongest objection to the multiverse comes from Lakens and colleagues, and it deserves to be stated at full strength. A research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated, and that quantity, together with the design and the assumptions that you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. It follows that a spread of results is evidence that most of the specifications are wrong, because they estimate something other than the quantity that you said you wanted, and not evidence of legitimate diversity. On that reading, a wide specification curve comes closer to an admission that the question was never specified than to a robustness check. [advance] Applied to the red-card study, a linear, a logistic and a Poisson model of one count of red cards are three claims about how the outcome was generated, which cannot all be right. I find the argument uncomfortable, and I think that it is largely right.
:::

The original comparison detects a gap of 20 points almost always (0.97), but one of 10 points less than half the time (0.48). The replication has 0.78 for 10 points.

::: notes
Power is the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. At a white share of sixty-one per cent, the original comparison, with about a hundred and eighty replies a group, detects a gap of twenty points almost every time, but its power is under one half for a gap of ten points and about seven in ten for thirteen. The replication, with three hundred and sixty-nine replies a group, has nearly eight in ten for a gap of ten points, so it would have found a gap of that size about four times in five, and a larger gap more often still, had there been one. When a study with modest power for realistic effects does reach significance, its estimate also tends to overstate the true effect, because only the lucky draws clear the bar, and the published interval runs from minus thirty to minus ten.

The first point comes from the article on the robustness study, which holds that analyses following a single path "should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses". A single path can be a good one, and the reader is still owed the space around it, so a report needs the chosen path and the alternatives together. Auspurg and Brüderl give the constructive recipe that we followed today: a precise question, assumptions drawn explicitly as a graph, a multiverse and a sensitivity analysis.
